Pasting and reflowing the boards

One sheet for both boards: the sensor board (two sides) and the CAN controller board (bottom only). Read it with the paste warming on the bench.

What is in play: Alpha OM-5100 leaded paste (35 g syringe), 4 mil stainless stencils, the 30 mil plastic spreaders, tweezers, the hot plate, isopropyl and lint-free wipes. The sensor board uses the MDF jig - Forstner recess, two 3 mm pins through the mounting holes and the stencil's matching holes. The controller board uses the acrylic jig set that came with its stencil.

How long you actually have

Hours, not minutes. A 15-minute rush is not real - this class of leaded no-clean paste stays workable on the board far longer than any one session needs:

Stage Window What actually goes wrong past it
Syringe out of the fridge warm 30-60 min before printing cold paste prints ragged and tears coming off the stencil
Printed deposits, waiting for parts a few hours deposits slowly dry out and lose their stick
Parts placed, waiting for the plate a few hours same - the tack that holds parts fades
Overnight no dried paste wets badly; wipe it off and print again

So: print, place at a comfortable pace, reflow in the same sitting. If life interrupts and a printed board has sat long enough to look dry or doubtful, the reset costs two minutes - wipe the board clean with isopropyl, dry it, print again. Never reflow a doubtful print; cleaning up bad joints costs far more.

Set up the board

The stencil has to lie dead flat on the board, and neither can move.

  • Sensor board: drop it into the MDF recess over the two pins, stencil onto the same pins. Push board and stencil toward the same corner before every pass - the pins have a few tenths of play, and one corner makes all four boards print the same.
  • Controller board: board into the acrylic jig pocket, jig taped to the bench. Lay the stencil on, slide it under good light until every opening sits centered on its pad, then tape one full edge of the stencil down as a hinge - from then on it lifts for inspection and drops back aligned.

Print the paste

  1. Push out a bead along the hinge edge, just outside the openings - about pencil thickness, a little wider than the pad field. Generous is right; the excess stays on the stencil.
  2. Spreader at 45-60 degrees, one firm continuous pass across every opening. The stencil should be wiped clean behind the stroke. The foil thickness meters the paste - even pressure matters, force does not.
  3. A missed spot gets one more full pass. Never dab at a single opening.
  4. Peel straight up, pivoting on the hinge or lifting off the pins - a clean vertical lift, not a slide.
  5. Look at the result: crisp separate bricks of paste, one per pad. Paste smeared between pads means wipe the board with isopropyl and print again.
  6. Wipe the stencil both sides with isopropyl now, not after reflow - paste dried into the openings is miserable to clear.

Place the parts

Tweezers, one part at a time, pressed just far enough in that the paste grips it. Close is good enough - when the solder melts, surface tension pulls every part square onto its pads. There is no clock running; get each one roughly centered and move on.

  • Sensor board: the chip side goes first - set the chip's pin-1 corner against the board marking before pressing it in.
  • Controller board: all 18 passives in one pass - 12 small caps, the 0805, the 100 nF, the four resistors.

Reflow on the hot plate

Watch the solder, not the dial.

  1. Board goes on the plate. Sensor board second side: board sits on the short pipe so the already-built chip side hangs clear; the copper still carries the heat. Pipe end faced flat so the board sits level.
  2. Bring the plate up. The paste goes dull and slumps first, then flows bright silver and every part settles and pulls itself square - that is the melt, 183 C at the joints.
  3. Count a few seconds after the last joint flows, then take the heat away - slide the board gently off, or plate off. Do not touch any part until the joints freeze; it takes seconds.
  4. First board of a batch is the pilot: find the dial setting that gets flow in a few minutes, write it on this sheet, photograph the placed and the reflowed board, and run the rest against the photos.

Dial setting that flows in a few minutes: __

After reflow

  • Every joint shiny with a small fillet, every part sitting flat. A bridge between pads comes off with the iron and wick.
  • The paste is a no-clean type: residue can stay. Isopropyl if it should look nice.
  • Syringe capped and back in the fridge. Jig and spreader wiped.

The jacks go on last, with the iron - they never ride the plate

Sensor board - the jack is surface-mount, soldered by iron. Its feet sit on pads; the joint is on the surface instead of in a hole, and the iron work is otherwise the same. Wire solder brings its own flux.

  1. Tin one shield pad - bare board, melt a small blob onto one of the two big shield pads.
  2. Set the jack down, hold it flat, and tack it - reheat that blob against the shell tab until it flows, hold still a second while it freezes.
  3. Check all eight feet sit centered on their pads. Off? Reheat the one tack and nudge - that is what tacking one joint first is for.
  4. Solder the other shell tab - the brass shell drinks heat: big tip, hold longer than feels natural, feed solder until it flows around the tab. Then re-do the first tack properly the same way.
  5. The eight feet, one at a time - tip touching foot and pad together, feed a little solder, one second each. A small shiny fillet climbing from pad onto foot is right. A bridge between neighbours comes off with wick.

Controller board - the jacks and the socket stack are through-hole. Pins through the board, soldered from the far side; the filter parts sit well back from the pin rows so the iron has room. Same tack-one-pin-and-check habit: one pin, check the part is seated flat and square, then the rest.
